opus-5.5.text:
I think the problem is that a vague prediction can't be wrong. If I say "the next paradigm will be something beyond scaling," or "agents will change everything," that sounds deep, but there's no way to check it, and it doesn't tell anyone what to do tomorrow morning. It has no content in a scientific sense.

In research, a prediction is only valuable if it's specific enough to be falsifiable and to guide action. Something like: "If we do RL on this kind of task with this kind of reward signal, we'll see generalization to these other tasks within a year." You can bet on that and build toward it. If it turns out wrong, you learn something. A vague prediction doesn't let you learn anything, because whatever happens, you can always reinterpret it as having come true.

Paradigm shifts are also rarely visible ahead of time in the form people imagine. When you look back at what actually moved the field, pretraining at scale, instruction tuning, RL from feedback, reasoning models, each one came from people working very concretely on a problem, noticing that something worked better than expected, and pushing on it. It didn't come from someone sitting back and announcing "the next paradigm is X." The people who made the shift usually weren't talking in grand terms. They were talking about loss curves, data, evals.

So when I hear broad statements about the future, my reaction is: what's the experiment? What would convince you you're wrong? If there's no answer, it's more like storytelling than prediction. Storytelling has its place, it can inspire people. But as a researcher I'd rather spend my energy on a narrow, concrete bet I can test, because that's how you find out where the real frontier is, rather than just talking about it.

r001.rationale: It says a vague prediction has no way to be checked and “can't be wrong,” so it cannot be meaningfully judged.

r002.rationale: It explains that whatever happens, the prediction can be reinterpreted as having come true.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because a prediction that can't be wrong isn't a prediction. If I say "the next paradigm will be something beyond scaling," or "agents will be the future," that sounds profound, but what does it actually constrain? Nothing. It's compatible with almost any outcome. In a year, whatever happens, I can say I called it.

The way I think about it comes from doing research. A useful idea has to be falsifiable and actionable. When we did ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the bet wasn't "reasoning will matter." The bet was very specific: if you interleave thinking and acting in this particular way, this benchmark goes up, and here's the mechanism. You can run that experiment. You can be wrong by Tuesday. That's what makes it meaningful.

And there's a second problem, which is that vague predictions are usually a way of avoiding the hard part. The hard part is never "will the paradigm change." Of course it will. The hard part is: what's the bottleneck right now, what's the concrete thing that's broken, and what would you build to fix it. If someone can't name the bottleneck, I don't think they actually have a view. They have a vibe.

I'd also say, in this field especially, the people who talk most confidently about "the next paradigm" tend to be the people furthest from the experiments. The people actually close to the models are usually more cautious, because they've seen how many clean stories fall apart when you look at the data.

So when I hear a grand prediction, my test is simple: tell me what evidence would change your mind, and tell me what you would do differently tomorrow because you believe it. If the answer to both is "nothing," then we're not talking about the future. We're just talking.

r001.rationale: It says a prediction that “can't be wrong” is not a prediction, because it constrains nothing and is compatible with almost any outcome.

r002.rationale: It observes that whatever happens in a year, the author can claim they called it.

astra-6.text:
Because if a prediction is vague enough, almost any outcome can be interpreted as confirming it. You say, “There will be a new paradigm,” but what exactly will change? What will it let us do that we can’t do today? And what would count as evidence that you’re wrong?

I think a useful prediction should constrain your decisions. If you believe something is going to happen, does that tell you which problem to work on, which experiment to run, or which assumption to question? If it doesn’t change any of those things, it’s hard to distinguish it from a slogan. I’d rather discuss a concrete bottleneck and how we might overcome it. Then we can actually test whether our understanding is right.

r001.rationale: It asks what would count as evidence the predictor is wrong and says a vague prediction is hard to distinguish from a slogan, explaining why it cannot be meaningfully judged.

r002.rationale: It says almost any outcome can be interpreted as confirming a vague prediction, so its author can claim vindication across different outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if a prediction is vague enough, almost any outcome can be interpreted as confirming it. Someone says, “The future is agents.” But what counts as an agent? What tasks can it actually complete? How reliably, and at what cost? Without those details, it’s hard to tell what the prediction means.

I find concrete questions more useful: What can’t today’s systems do? What’s the bottleneck? What experiment would tell us whether an approach works? You can have a big vision, but it becomes useful when it leads to something you can test—and potentially discover you were wrong about.

r001.rationale: It says a sufficiently vague prediction can be interpreted as confirming almost any outcome, so it cannot be meaningfully tested or shown wrong.

r002.rationale: It explicitly notes that almost any outcome can be read as confirmation, allowing the prediction’s author to claim vindication across different outcomes.
